extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and theatre practitioners interested in the history, features, and analysis of mid-20th-century dramatic movements (Theatre of the Absurd).
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative features for creating or analysing plays in the Theatre of the Absurd tradition—characteristics, language, plot, form, themes, and intended theatrical effects associated with absurdist drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existentialist focus and depiction of meaninglessness
rubrics_metrics.description: The plays focus largely on ideas of existentialism and express what happens when human existence lacks meaning or purpose and communication breaks down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should foreground the human situation as meaningless or absurd (Camus' Myth of Sisyphus is cited). This manifests as characters confronting purposelessness, alienation, or being 'cut off from religious, metaphysical, and transcendental roots.' Examples: many of Beckett's plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclical/round structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the plays is typically a round shape, with the finishing point the same as the starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plots and scenes often repeat or return to their starting conditions (cyclical plots). Examples: Endgame begins where it ends; Waiting for Godot features repetitive waiting and cycles of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment of logical construction in favour of irrational/illogical speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical construction and argument give way to irrational and illogical speech and to the ultimate conclusion—silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue and dramatic logic may deliberately defy cause-and-effect or coherent argument, leading to breakdowns that underscore meaninglessness. Use of silence as an endpoint is a recognized device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragicomedy: broad comedy mixed with horror or tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Some characteristics coincide in many of the plays: broad comedy, often similar to vaudeville, mixed with horrific or tragic images. The mode of most 'absurdist' plays is tragicomedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend comic mechanisms (farce, vaudeville, wordplay) with bleak, tragic, or horrifying elements so that laughter and dread coexist. Shakespearean influences and references (e.g., tragic moments arising out of comedy) are noted as precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as automatons, stereotypes, or figures trapped in routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are frequently stereotypical, archetypal, or flat character types; many appear as automatons stuck in routines speaking only in cliché. The more complex characters are in crisis because the world around them is incomprehensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters who exhibit repetitive, meaningless actions or are reduced to types. The 'pseudocouple' pairing (two interdependent characters) is a recurring device (e.g., Vladimir and Estragon). Examples: Pozzo and Lucky, Hamm and Clov, Berenger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language characterised by clichés, wordplay, nonsense, and musical/phonetic qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is often full of clichés, wordplay, and nonsense; language frequently gains a certain phonetic, rhythmical, almost musical quality, opening up a wide range of often comedic playfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empty clichés, nonsensical speech, vaudeville-style wordplay, or rhythmical/phonetic arrangement to show the inadequacy of language and to create comic or unsettling effects. Examples: The Bald Soprano (clichés), Lucky's speech in Godot (nonsense), Tardieu's musical arrangement of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elliptical dialogue, silences, and 'Pinter pause' style devices
rubrics_metrics.description: In other cases, the dialogue is purposefully elliptical; ellipsis, dashes, and pauses replace direct statements. Harold Pinter is famous for the 'Pinter pause'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ ellipses, pauses, and truncated exchanges to create evasiveness, stalled communication, and implied menace. This can heighten tension and meaning through absence rather than explicit exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as nontraditional: repetition, absence, menace, metamorphosis, unresolved mysteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional plot structures are rarely a consideration. Plots can consist of absurd repetition of cliché and routine; often there is a menacing outside force that remains a mystery; plots may involve unexplained metamorphosis or absence and unresolved mysteries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forego conventional causality and resolution—use repetitive routines (Godot), invisible/absent presences (The Chairs), unexplained transformations (Amédée), or enigmatic menaces (The Birthday Party). Emphasize emptiness, nothingness, and open-endedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody or dismissal of realism and the 'well-made play'
rubrics_metrics.description: Either a parody or dismissal of realism and the concept of the 'well-made play'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject realistic character psychology, linear plot mechanics, and tidy resolutions; instead parody or subvert bourgeois theatrical conventions to expose theatrical artifice and philosophical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal experimentation and avant-garde influences
rubrics_metrics.description: As an experimental form of theatre, many theatre of the absurd playwrights employ techniques borrowed from earlier innovators: nonsense poets, Brechtian distancing, Pirandello's metatheatre, dream plays, pataphysics, surrealism, Dadaism, and Artaud's Theatre of Cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate metatheatrical elements (plays-within-plays, roleplaying, breaking the fourth wall), surreal imagery, pataphysical conceits, Brechtian estrangement or Artaudian visceral techniques to upset audience expectations and theatrical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metatheatre and self-reflexivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many absurdists use meta-theatrical techniques to explore role fulfillment, fate, and the theatricality of theatre (e.g., Six Characters in Search of an Author, Rosencrantz & Guildenstern Are Dead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ self-referential structures, characters aware of their dramatic status, or plays that embed other plays; use these devices to question identity, authorship, and the boundary between performance and reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devaluation of language in favour of stage tableau and visceral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of absurdist theater becomes secondary to the poetry of the concrete and objectified images of the stage. Much of Beckett's plays devalue language for the sake of the striking tableau. Artaud argued for theatre's visceral impact over literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise strong visual tableaux, choreography, sounds, and stage objects over expository dialogue; allow images, movement, and physical staging to carry theme and emotional force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic intent: to shock complacency and evoke a liberating laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The Theatre of the Absurd attacks the comfortable certainties of religious or political orthodoxy. It aims to shock its audience out of complacency, to bring it face to face with the harsh facts of the human situation... the Theatre of the Absurd does not provoke tears of despair but the laughter of liberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design theatrical strategies that unsettle ideological certainties and provoke critical reflection; aim for an effect that mixes discomfort with relief or liberating laughter rather than mere despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of abusive or menacing nonsense as a power/violence device
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsense may also be used abusively, as in Pinter's The Birthday Party when characters torture another with apparently nonsensical questions and non-sequiturs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit nonsensical language and non-sequiturs as instruments of intimidation, psychological torture, or power play within dramatic interactions.
